- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000ms / 30 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.

Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. ## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call
  `new_tab()` again in every script.

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups

# Atomization brief (shared by every Flint ingest agent)

Read this whole file before writing anything. It holds the rules the Harries review taught (2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes). The review gate will check every rule here.

## Schema

Follow `C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\ingest-book\SKILL.md` exactly: `_domain.md`, `_book.md` (map and resume checkpoint, updated after EACH chapter or unit), and entries named `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md` with kind one of principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim. Use the frontmatter keys exactly as the skill gives them. The body has **What it is** / **Why it works** / **When to apply** / **When NOT to apply** (mandatory, non-trivial) / **Example** / **Related**.

Style reference, read before writing: `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library\strength-and-conditioning\fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer\case-study--isometric-sprinter-and-hurdler.md`, plus one principle file in the same folder.

## Voices: label every one

- **The source author's statements are plain text.**
- **Eric's views** (from `docs/method-baseline.md` or his reviews) are prefixed "Eric's baseline:" or "Eric's review:".
- **Your own reasoning, application or synthesis** is prefixed "Inference:".
- **Nothing unlabeled that the author did not say.** The most common failures: a judgment from Eric's review written as if the author said it; a mechanism the author never gave presented as "why it works" (write "The author gives no mechanism. Inference: ..."); an invented example.

## Lessons from the Supertraining Chapter 1 review (2026-09-26: 30 FIX, 1 NO-GO of 41)

- **Keep the source's internal contradictions.** When a book says X on one page and not-X on another, record both with their pages and set `contested`. Never pick one side silently. The NO-GO entry reversed the book's SJ-CMJ strength-deficit rule because the book states it both ways.
- **Name the right voice.** In co-authored books, write "the authors" unless a passage clearly belongs to one author. A passage that names Verkhoshansky in the third person is Siff writing.
- **Keep `proven` rare and scoped.** Scope it to the replicated core (for example, "Hill's force-velocity curve"), never the whole entry, and mark any disputed sentence inside it. Four of eight `proven` ratings were lowered.
- **No mechanism the source does not give.** About a dozen "Why it works" sections supplied physiology the book never states. Label it "Inference:" or leave it out.
- **Do not add "well established" or "modern research shows" without a citation.** Name the paper, or delete the phrase.

## Lessons from the 2026-09-27 review wave (Supertraining Ch2-3, Issurin Ch3, Bondarchuk, Evans, Old Bull)

- **Invented Examples are the most common failure.** 34 of 36 Supertraining Ch2-3a Examples were unlabelled inventions. Use the source's own example where it gives one; otherwise start the Example with "Inference:".
- **"Verified against the page image" means you opened the image.** Four Issurin Ch3 entries claimed it for figures they had misread (Fig 3.7 inverted, a Table 3.7 row swapped). Sparse slides are not "bare diagrams" until you have looked.
- **Name the population and method the source gives.** Bondarchuk's data are 7,000+ native and foreign athletes, questionnaires, r >= 0.349, steroid-free; entries that said "Soviet athletes" were wrong everywhere.
- **Check what a cited paper actually says.** Issurin 2016's critique targets Verkhoshansky's concentrated-unidirectional model, not Issurin's A-T-R; Herzog & Leonard 2000 shows force enhancement, against the book's sentence. When the book misreports a study, record both.
- **No review history in entries.** "Prior version", "corrected from a NO-GO finding" and similar belong in `staging/fixes_*_applied.md`, never in the entry body.
- **Fix logs must match the files.** One fixer log claimed fixes that were not made. Fixers run their own grep checks and paste the output.
- **Section headers use the vault form** `**What it is** —` (with the em dash). Do not add suffixes such as ": mandatory". Em dashes are banned only in titles and body text. Never wrap a `[[wikilink]]` across lines.

## Evidence

- Every number, definition and quote carries a checkable locator: PDF page (and printed page if it differs), or file plus timestamp. Never write "confirmed in PDF" unless you opened that page.
- Never invent a number. Keep ambiguity visible: mark unclear audio or OCR as unclear, and do not harmonize two conflicting numbers from the source; record both with their locators.
- OCR sources (`staging/ocr/*.md`): pages listed as low_confidence in the header must be checked against the page image before any number from them is cited. Use the Read tool on the PDF page, or render it.
- **OCR confidence scores miss the worst errors** (checked 2026-09-27). Zatsiorsky 2e: the OCR interleaves the two columns and the sidebars line by line, so its text is not readable prose; use it only to find content, and read and quote from the page image. *CFTS*: single-column prose that mostly reads in order, but upside-down lines come out as gibberish, some lines are dropped, and figures are scrambled, all at "0 low-confidence pages". For any OCR source, quote only after checking the page image, and read every figure and table from the image.

## Confidence

- Practitioner courses and lectures: ceiling `supported`.
- Books: `proven` only for established, widely replicated physiology or mechanics. Soviet-era or single-lab empirical findings and training prescriptions: `supported` at most. `untested` for single cases and anecdotes. `contested` where another library source or modern evidence disagrees (say which).

## Dedup and converge

Before each entry, grep `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library` and the staging library (`C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\staging\library`) for the concept. If it is covered, add a new entry only for a genuinely new angle, and link the existing one in Related. List reciprocal-link suggestions in your final report. Never edit files in the vault or another agent's staging folder.

## Baylor context

Read `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\docs\method-baseline.md` (approved). Use it in When to apply, labelled "Eric's baseline:". Department names: Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine, Applied Performance. Plain style, no em dashes. Use commas, colons and parentheses.

## Scope and output

- Write ONLY into your assigned staging folder. No git, no vault edits.
- Stop at a chapter or unit boundary. It is better to finish fewer chapters well; the `_book.md` checkpoint lets the next batch resume.
- Final reply: entries by kind and by confidence; chapters or units done and pending with page ranges; reciprocal-link suggestions; unclear or contradictory spots in the source; anything you could not read.

**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally reports a league-wide study, "under review" at the time of the talk, using public MLB data (z_6M5r7031A [11:44] to [12:14]).
- **Window:** 2004 to 2014, chosen so that players who had surgery in 2014 had time to return (z_6M5r7031A [11:44] to [12:14]).
- **Counts:** about 200 surgeries, and on average 180 days of MLB-calendar time missed (z_6M5r7031A [12:14]). About half the players were starters and half relievers, with a small proportion of closers (z_6M5r7031A [12:44]).
- **Total:** adjusted to 2017 levels, "half a billion dollars" of salary lost over the period to rehab alone (z_6M5r7031A [12:44]).
- **Excluded:** medical, travel and rehab costs; downtime before the surgery; lost team wins; trade value; and every minor league player (z_6M5r7031A [12:44] to [13:44]). He speculates the full cost might be 1 billion or 1.5 billion and says "I don't know" (z_6M5r7031A [13:44]).
- **Per player:** medical cost of about $50,000, which he calls conservative (z_6M5r7031A [11:13]). (Untested: bare assertion, no method given.)
- **Salary per WAR:** it "balloons" after surgery and does not return to the pre-surgery level until 3 years after the pitcher returns (z_6M5r7031A [10:43]). In Q&A he calls the salary-over-WAR calculation "relatively back of the envelope" and not adjusted (z_6M5r7031A [28:27]). (Untested: back-of-envelope, unadjusted.)

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism; this is an accounting of public salary data. Inference: it counts only direct salary during rehab, which is why the number is a floor on the speaker's own account.

**When to apply** — As an example of costing an injury type from public records by counting time missed and attaching a value. Eric's baseline: no formal injury-risk model is attributed to Eric (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Inference: a Baylor version would count games and practices missed by injury type and position group with Athletic Medicine, with no salary figure.

**When NOT to apply** — The study was under review, not published, at the time. Baylor athletes have no player salaries, so dollar figures and dollars per WAR do not transfer to college. The salary-per-WAR calculation is unadjusted and the speaker's own words are "back of the envelope." The 180-day figure is MLB calendar time. It is professional baseball pitchers only, and it counts surgeries, not all injuries.

**Example** — The speaker's own: about 200 surgeries over 2004 to 2014 and 180 MLB-calendar days missed on average, summing to half a billion 2017 dollars (z_6M5r7031A [12:14] to [12:44]).

143:- No formal injury-risk model (ACWR, tissue-capacity tracking, a biomechanical screening protocol with defined red flags) is attributed to Eric anywhere in this corpus; the detailed treatment of ACWR and injury-risk modeling that does exist (Clemson curriculum) is reference material only, not confirmed Baylor practice. === claim--concussion-vulnerability-window-longer-than-return-rules-assumed.md
# The post-concussion "window of vulnerability" is longer than return-to-play practice assumed

**What it is** — The speaker defines the window of vulnerability as the period after a concussion in which further physical or cognitive trauma is "much more damaging", slower to recover from and may lead to permanent deficits; the comparison used is playing on a broken leg (npgdKKdJSww [04:04], [04:34]). The speaker says the window is "dramatically" longer than believed:
- In 2008 athletes were still being sent back within 15 minutes if symptoms cleared on the sideline (npgdKKdJSww [12:43]).
- The window in rats is 7 to 10 days (npgdKKdJSww [12:43], [13:13]).
- Research tests (magnetic resonance spectroscopy, fMRI, blood flow, evoked potentials) find that "no one seems to recover to baseline" on the hardest tests within 30 days, so "their brain is abnormal" (npgdKKdJSww [13:13], [13:43]).
- The working rule described is that an athlete abnormal against the athlete's own baseline neuropsychological test cannot go back in (npgdKKdJSww [13:43]).

The speaker cites a recent case (a pro hockey star still out; a basketball star back in three days) as a failure to respect the window (npgdKKdJSww [04:34], [05:04]). The speaker flags the claim as broad: with little time, broad concepts are being used and the audience is asked not to criticize the science (npgdKKdJSww [13:13]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's mechanism is that a concussion "starts a Cascade of events" that leaves the brain vulnerable (npgdKKdJSww [04:34]); the cascade is not described. Inference: the rat figure and the abnormal research scans are indirect evidence for a human clinical window, and the speaker moves from them to a longer clinical window without showing the link.

**When to apply** — As a reason to be wary of any return-to-play criterion built on clinical symptom clearance alone, and when a stakeholder asks why concussion return takes longer than other injuries. It is context for Athletic Medicine's process, not a rule for Applied Performance testing.

Eric's baseline: Applied Performance does not assess readiness in return to play: "We don't assess readiness. The template answers that" (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q22). The baseline holds no concussion criteria and no recovery-window rules.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use "no one recovers within 30 days" as a clinical return criterion: abnormal research imaging is not the same as unreadiness, and the speaker admits to broad strokes and to the 60-day figure being a hypothetical (npgdKKdJSww [13:43]). The rat window is animal data, with no human study shown. The speaker's "15 minutes in 2008" is a statement of past practice, not a cited study. The talk is from 2012; consensus guidance has changed, so check current guidelines with Athletic Medicine. Return-to-play decisions on concussion are medical decisions.

**Example** — The speaker's own: a basketball star "back in three days" after a concussion, described as "ridiculous" (npgdKKdJSww [05:04]); the speaker's view, not a measured case.

**Related** — [[claim--diagnosed-concussion-rates-undercount-survey-and-observer-rates]]; [[claim--perfect-concussion-detection-would-sideline-one-fifth-of-players]] (the availability cost of taking this window seriously); [[principle--competitive-exposure-required-before-return-to-play]] (Harries: what return-to-play criteria should include for non-concussion injuries; compare, do not merge).

=== claim--diagnosed-concussion-rates-undercount-survey-and-observer-rates.md
# Diagnosed concussion rates sit far below what surveys and sideline observers find

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Chris nowinsky", who also gives his background as a former Harvard football player and pro wrestler, npgdKKdJSww [01:00]) says that programs with athletic trainers diagnose about 5% of athletes per year in contact and collision sports, "one out of 20", while anonymous end-of-season surveys that leave out the word "concussion" and ask about symptoms after blows give numbers "more like 50%" (npgdKKdJSww [06:04]). He cites three further results, all second-hand and with garbled study names:
- A study (caption "langbert") in which the average person suffered "three dings per season" (npgdKKdJSww [06:34]).
- A hockey study (caption "eckan") of 16 to 21 year olds in which a doctor placed in the stands liberally pulled players who looked off and tested them with the standard tools: the speaker reports the study author found 35% ("one-third were pulled out") versus 5% in the usual trainer-only group, "seven times as many" concussions (npgdKKdJSww [06:34], [07:04]).
- An observer study in which stand observers saw about half the symptoms players reported; the captions give 33 versus 54 for a women's sample, with the unit unstated, so the figures are unclear (npgdKKdJSww [07:04]).

From these he estimates "we are probably diagnosing between two and 10% of concussions" (npgdKKdJSww [07:34]). The estimate is the speaker's own, not a measured rate.

**Why it works** — The speaker's mechanism is that the injury cannot be seen: concussion does not show on standard CT or MRI and diagnosis rests on signs and symptoms, so sports "get by" without removing athletes the way they would for a visible injury (npgdKKdJSww [05:04], [07:34]). Inference: a diagnosis count measures reporting and detection effort as much as incidence, which is why putting a doctor in the stands moved the count sevenfold.

**When to apply** — When someone quotes a diagnosed-concussion rate as the incidence of the injury, or when judging whether an Athletic Medicine count captures most events. Inference: an anonymous symptom survey at season end, asked without the word "concussion", is the comparison the speaker's own data points to.

Eric's baseline: Applied Performance's part in return to play is testing and progression with shared loading decisions (Eric, interview 2026-09-28, Q4: "Testing and progression. I collaborate on loading and progression decisions when needed. It doesn't really end." Explicit), and no formal injury-risk model is in use (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). The baseline holds no concussion criteria, so this entry is a comparison point, not a method Eric uses.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not read 50% as the rate of medically diagnosable concussion; surveys count self-reported symptoms after blows. The hockey sample is 16 to 21 year olds, and the speaker gives no sample sizes for any of the three studies. The speaker discloses a consultant role and a financial tie to the owner of the King-Devick test (npgdKKdJSww [00:30]). The talk is from 2012, so detection practice and rules have changed since. Do not carry the rates to Baylor football without Athletic Medicine's own counts. Anything diagnostic belongs to Athletic Medicine; Applied Performance does not set concussion criteria.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the hockey study, where adding one observer with pull-out authority took the identified share from 5% to 35% (npgdKKdJSww [06:34], [07:04]).

**Related** — [[framework--impact-alert-threshold-and-sideline-test-pairing]]; [[claim--perfect-concussion-detection-would-sideline-one-fifth-of-players]] (the speaker's own consequence of closing this gap); [[claim--concussion-vulnerability-window-longer-than-return-rules-assumed]]; [[funk-2025-an-analysis-of-guardian-cap-use-and-changes-in-the-concussion-rate-in-national-football-le]] (NFL preseason practice concussion rates, an exposure-based cohort).

=== claim--perfect-concussion-detection-would-sideline-one-fifth-of-players.md
# If every concussion were caught and managed strictly, about one in five players would be out at any time

**What it is** — A back-of-envelope availability model. The speaker, using the survey figure that about half of athletes have a concussion each year, takes a 50-person football team with half concussed (25 players) and 10 days out each: 250 days, "about 4% of playing days", "not completely disruptive" (npgdKKdJSww [12:12]). The speaker then argues recovery is longer than 10 days (see the vulnerability-window entry) and reruns it at 60 days out: "21% of playing days", "one out of five athletes out at all times", about four of a football team's starters and one hockey starter at any moment, not counting repeat concussions (npgdKKdJSww [13:43], [14:14]). The speaker's conclusion is that either medical guidelines get much looser ("which won't happen") or the games change, starting with how much contact they contain (npgdKKdJSww [14:45], [22:58]).

The speaker says the math was done "on the plane" and that "the science is iffy" on the 10-day figure (npgdKKdJSww [12:12]).

**Why it works** — It is arithmetic on three assumed inputs: incidence, days out, and playing days in a season. The speaker gives the first two and not the third. Inference: 250 days equal 4% only if the team has about 6,250 player-days (50 players over about 125 days), and the 60-day case then gives 1,500 days over 6,250, or 24%, not the 21% the speaker states; the two figures are not exactly proportional and the denominator is not shown. Treat both as rough.

**When to apply** — As a reminder to test a proposed detection or return-to-play standard against roster availability before adopting it: ask what the standard would cost in player-days if applied to every case.

Eric's baseline: Applied Performance's role in return to performance is to supply information that supports Athletic Medicine and Athletic Performance decisions (Explicit, Playbook p.6), and Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q22): "We don't assess readiness. The template answers that." (Explicit). Inference: an availability estimate like this one is the kind of information Applied Performance could supply; the clearance standard itself stays with Athletic Medicine.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use the 4% or 21% figures as estimates for Baylor or for any real team. The 50% incidence is a survey figure from the speaker's other studies; the 10-day and 60-day recoveries are assumptions, and the 60-day case is the speaker's hypothetical of what very sensitive tests might demand, not a clinical standard. The model ignores repeat concussions, position differences and substitutions. It is a 2012 talk, and the speaker discloses a consultant role and a test-owner tie (npgdKKdJSww [00:30]).

**Example** — The speaker's own: a 50-person football team, 25 concussed, 60 days out each, "four guys out on your football team every week out of your starting group" (npgdKKdJSww [14:14]).

**Related** — [[claim--diagnosed-concussion-rates-undercount-survey-and-observer-rates]] (source of the 50% input); [[claim--concussion-vulnerability-window-longer-than-return-rules-assumed]] (source of the 30 to 60 day input); [[claim--practice-contact-is-the-largest-exposure-lever-in-football]] (the lever the speaker proposes in response).

# Cutting contact in practice is the main lever on head-impact exposure

**What it is** — The speaker's stated focus is "reducing hitting in practice", the "number one way" to restrict total counts, because in football "up to 75%" of brain trauma exposure happens in practice (npgdKKdJSww [19:23]). The speaker gives three policy moves as evidence that people are "buying in":
- In the NFL collective bargaining talks the players' union pushed for 14 practice days with contact in 18 weeks (npgdKKdJSww [19:23]).
- The Ivy League followed: NCAA rules allow five days of hitting a week and the Ivy League chose two, with an intent to push lower (npgdKKdJSww [19:54]).
- Pop Warner's executive director announced a plan to cut hitting from six hours a week to two by the next season (npgdKKdJSww [19:54]).

The speaker says "I was on both committees" (the captions do not name which) and "pushed these like crazy" (npgdKKdJSww [19:54]), and that some limit on how many contact sports a child plays in a year is likely to follow (npgdKKdJSww [20:24]).

**Why it works** — The speaker states that most of the exposure comes in practice (npgdKKdJSww [19:23]) and gives no further reasoning. Inference: practices outnumber games, so most hits occur there. The 75% figure comes with no source or method in the talk. Inference: contact in practice is also the exposure a program controls directly, which is why it is a lever where game contact is not.

**When to apply** — When a contact-practice schedule is being set or reviewed and the discussion is about how many contact periods, not about equipment. Inference: Applied Performance could log contact periods per practice by position group (practice minutes with contact, not impacts) and report them weekly to Athletic Medicine and coaches, as a record, not a cap.

Eric's baseline: "Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver" (Inferred (transcript)). In the in-season game week, lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q15). The baseline holds no contact-practice rule and no concussion criteria.

**When NOT to apply** — The 75% is an assertion, and it is "up to" for football only (npgdKKdJSww [19:23]). The three policy examples are the speaker's account of NFL, Ivy League and youth practice, with the speaker involved in two of them; none reports an outcome. College or Baylor practice schedules are not described, and contact definitions would have to be agreed with coaches. The talk gives no evidence that limiting contact reduces concussions; it gives the exposure logic and the policy trend. A contact-practice decision is the coaching staff's with Athletic Medicine; Applied Performance supplies the count.

**Example** — The speaker's own: Pop Warner moving from six hours of weekly contact to two (npgdKKdJSww [19:54]).

**Related** — [[framework--hit-count-as-exposure-budget-modeled-on-pitch-count]]; [[claim--perfect-concussion-detection-would-sideline-one-fifth-of-players]]; [[funk-2025-an-analysis-of-guardian-cap-use-and-changes-in-the-concussion-rate-in-national-football-le]] (NFL preseason practice concussion rates).

=== framework--hit-count-as-exposure-budget-modeled-on-pitch-count.md
# A "hit count" for head impacts, modeled on baseball's pitch count

**What it is** — The speaker proposes counting head impacts the way baseball counts pitches: a cumulative exposure with a limit and rest, because subconcussive blows (hits that cause no clinical symptoms and pass the usual tests) may still injure the brain (npgdKKdJSww [15:46], [16:16]). He says that at a Super Bowl the NFL "let us have the press conference" announcing the goal of a hit count (npgdKKdJSww [16:48]). The steps he gives:
- Model it on the pitch count: age caps (75 pitches at age 10, 85 at 11) plus mandatory rest (three days after 61 pitches). He admits those numbers are "clearly not based on much science" ("every number ends on five"), and accepts that as good enough to protect people (npgdKKdJSww [17:19]).
- Accept that low-level bumps are probably harmless, that damage is probable from some level up to concussive levels, and that the middle is unknown; lowering the number of hits lowers concussion risk too (npgdKKdJSww [17:50]).
- Count with sensors: he says college football players take "somewhere between 500 and 1,000 blows", one high school player took 2,235 blows above 10 G in 3 months, hockey players average a few hundred, and some near a thousand (npgdKKdJSww [18:20]).
- Pick a line, knowing "no one knows what that is" (npgdKKdJSww [18:20], [18:51]).
- Look by position: average force is about the same across football positions but totals differ: wide receivers under 400, linemen near or well over 1,000. An arbitrary cap of 500 would leave linemen, running backs and linebackers unable to finish a season (npgdKKdJSww [18:51]).

He also adds exposure across sports: 2,000 in football, about 1,000 in ice hockey (caption "a th000 on ice hockey", garbled), a couple of thousand in soccer, "probably no child" should take 5,000 head hits a year (npgdKKdJSww [20:24]), and a soccer-heading study (caption "Lipton", unpublished, diffusion tensor imaging) in which players taking up to 5,000 headers a year with over 1,300 were more likely to have cognitive and imaging abnormalities in their early 30s (npgdKKdJSww [20:55]).

**Why it works** — His analogy is that "your elbow will wear out" with too many throws and "your brain will wear out" with too many hits, with the brain more important (npgdKKdJSww [16:48]). He gives no dose-response data for the brain. Inference: the idea works as a monitoring structure (count, cap, rest) even before a safe number is known, because it makes exposure visible by position and by week.

**When to apply** — When building an exposure report by position group, where counts per athlete are the output and a cap is not yet set. Inference: a weekly count by position, shown to Athletic Medicine and the coaching staff, is the decision aid; a cap needs Baylor's own data over several seasons.

Eric's baseline: abrupt, large changes in volume and intensity are treated as an injury-risk driver and progressions are kept smooth (Inferred, transcript, speaker unconfirmed, course team position); there is no formal injury-risk model (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12), and ACWR is looked at but not trusted ("raw, has error, is misleading, and lacks context"). The course material also warns that heavy load-monitoring culture can push teams toward under-preparing athletes (Inferred, transcript, course team position); the speaker gives no evidence on that trade-off.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not set a cap from any number in the talk: the speaker says no one knows the line, the 5,000-header study is unpublished and from soccer, and the sensor counts are a few cases in football and hockey with no validity data for the devices. The talk's youth examples (Pop Warner, a high school player) do not give college thresholds. The speaker says some marketing of impact sensors was "unethical" (npgdKKdJSww [08:04]). Using GPS-unit collision output as a head-impact proxy is an inference this talk does not support.

**Example** — The speaker's own positional comparison: receivers under 400 impacts, linemen near or over 1,000 at about the same average force (npgdKKdJSww [18:51]). The caption at [18:51] ("th000") is garbled; the figure is as read.

**Related** — [[framework--impact-alert-threshold-and-sideline-test-pairing]]; [[claim--practice-contact-is-the-largest-exposure-lever-in-football]]; [[framework--pitch-smart-count-and-rest-guideline-program]] (the baseball pitch-count program this one is modeled on, from a 2017 talk); [[claim--youth-pitching-over-100-innings-triples-serious-injury-risk]] (the exposure evidence behind pitch counts, from a 2015 talk).

=== framework--impact-alert-threshold-and-sideline-test-pairing.md
# Setting an impact-alert threshold: the S-curve and the sideline test it depends on

**What it is** — The speaker's way of reasoning about a helmet, headband or mouthpiece sensor with a red-light and green-light alert (npgdKKdJSww [08:04]). Risk of concussion against linear acceleration is an S-curve: the speaker knows of no concussion at 10 G, and concussion "everyone's going to get" at 300 G, with only a curve in between, so any alert line is arbitrary (npgdKKdJSww [08:04], [08:35]). The speaker walks the trade-off:
- Line at 50 G: the light "going off all the time", and every flagged athlete needs an evaluation.
- Line at 100 G: fewer alerts, but concussions at 60 or 70 G are missed.
- Line at 150 G: "once every few games", and "you're really not helping anybody" because most concussions happen at lower levels (npgdKKdJSww [08:35], [09:06]).

The alert is only usable if the follow-up test is fast. The speaker wants a sideline test under one minute so the line can be set low (the speaker mentions 80 or 100 G) without disrupting the game (npgdKKdJSww [09:06], [09:36]). The existing 20-minute evaluation (caption "SC stat too", likely SCAT2) "has never been validated" and its parts cannot decide return to play alone, and at a low yield (the speaker says "10%" actually concussed) "no one's going to use it" (npgdKKdJSww [09:36], [10:06]). The one fast test the speaker calls promising is King-Devick: two published papers (boxers, MMA fighters, college athletes at Penn) found concussions in under one minute by comparing to baseline (npgdKKdJSww [11:41]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives the logic of false alarms against misses but no data on any particular line. Inference: the threshold choice sets a false-alarm rate, and the false-alarm rate is only tolerable if the confirmation step is cheap, which makes the confirmation step the binding design constraint.

**When to apply** — Before anyone proposes alerts from impact sensors, GPS-unit collision counts or any single-number flag: state the line, the expected alerts per game, who evaluates each one, and how long that takes.

Eric's baseline: a measurement earns its place only if it answers a question someone has ("If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place," interview 2026-09-28, Q3, Explicit), and data collection is judged on cost against insight (Explicit, SportSmith 2026-02-19). Inference: an alert with no cheap follow-up fails both tests.

**When NOT to apply** — The speaker discloses a financial relationship with the owner of the King-Devick test (npgdKKdJSww [00:30]), and the "promising" claim rests on two papers the speaker does not name. The 10 G and 300 G anchors are stated without a source. The talk is from 2012 and the SCAT2 and King-Devick remarks may be out of date; check current guidelines. The caption "45C evaluation" at [11:41] to [12:12] is garbled. Return-to-play decisions belong to Athletic Medicine.

**Example** — The speaker's own: a line of 80 to 100 G with a one-minute baseline-comparison test, so that "you know immediately whether or not they can go back in" (npgdKKdJSww [09:36]). The speaker says this does not exist yet ("right now we don't have that").

**Related** — [[claim--diagnosed-concussion-rates-undercount-survey-and-observer-rates]]; [[framework--hit-count-as-exposure-budget-modeled-on-pitch-count]]; [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]] (Old Bull: what a sensor measures versus what is inferred from it).

**What it is** — The speaker's stated focus is "reducing hitting in practice", the "number one way" to restrict total counts, because in football "up to 75%" of brain trauma exposure happens in practice (npgdKKdJSww [19:23]). - The Ivy League followed: NCAA rules allow five days of hitting a week and the Ivy League chose two, with an intent to push lower (npgdKKdJSww [19:54]).

The speaker says "I was on both committees" (the captions do not name which) and "pushed these like crazy" (npgdKKdJSww [19:54]), and that some limit on how many contact sports a child plays in a year is likely to follow (npgdKKdJSww [20:24]).

# A "hit count" for head impacts, modeled on baseball's pitch count

**What it is** — The speaker proposes counting head impacts the way baseball counts pitches: a cumulative exposure with a limit and rest, because subconcussive blows (hits that cause no clinical symptoms and pass the usual tests) may still injure the brain (npgdKKdJSww [15:46], [16:16]). He says that at a Super Bowl the NFL "let us have the press conference" announcing the goal of a hit count (npgdKKdJSww [16:48]). The steps he gives:
- Model it on the pitch count: age caps (75 pitches at age 10, 85 at 11) plus mandatory rest (three days after 61 pitches). He admits those numbers are "clearly not based on much science" ("every number ends on five"), and accepts that as good enough to protect people (npgdKKdJSww [17:19]).
- Accept that low-level bumps are probably harmless, that damage is probable from some level up to concussive levels, and that the middle is unknown; lowering the number of hits lowers concussion risk too (npgdKKdJSww [17:50]).
- Count with sensors: he says college football players take "somewhere between 500 and 1,000 blows", one high school player took 2,235 blows above 10 G in 3 months, hockey players average a few hundred, and some near a thousand (npgdKKdJSww [18:20]).
- Pick a line, knowing "no one knows what that is" (npgdKKdJSww [18:20], [18:51]).
- Look by position: average force is about the same across football positions but totals differ: wide receivers under 400, linemen near or well over 1,000. An arbitrary cap of 500 would leave linemen, running backs and linebackers unable to finish a season (npgdKKdJSww [18:51]).

He also adds exposure across sports: 2,000 in football, about 1,000 in ice hockey (caption "a th000 on ice hockey", garbled), a couple of thousand in soccer, "probably no child" should take 5,000 head hits a year (npgdKKdJSww [20:24]), and a soccer-heading study (caption "Lipton", unpublished, diffusion tensor imaging) in which players taking up to 5,000 headers a year with over 1,300 were more likely to have cognitive and imaging abnormalities in their early 30s (npgdKKdJSww [20:55]).

**Why it works** — His analogy is that "your elbow will wear out" with too many throws and "your brain will wear out" with too many hits, with the brain more important (npgdKKdJSww [16:48]). He gives no dose-response data for the brain. Inference: the idea works as a monitoring structure (count, cap, rest) even before a safe number is known, because it makes exposure visible by position and by week.

**When to apply** — When building an exposure report by position group, where counts per athlete are the output and a cap is not yet set. Inference: a weekly count by position, shown to Athletic Medicine and the coaching staff, is the decision aid; a cap needs Baylor's own data over several seasons.

Eric's baseline: abrupt, large changes in volume and intensity are treated as an injury-risk driver and progressions are kept smooth (Inferred, transcript, speaker unconfirmed, course team position); there is no formal injury-risk model (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12), and ACWR is looked at but not trusted ("raw, has error, is misleading, and lacks context"). The course material also warns that heavy load-monitoring culture can push teams toward under-preparing athletes (Inferred, transcript, course team position); the speaker gives no evidence on that trade-off.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not set a cap from any number in the talk: the speaker says no one knows the line, the 5,000-header study is unpublished and from soccer, and the sensor counts are a few cases in football and hockey with no validity data for the devices. The talk's youth examples (Pop Warner, a high school player) do not give college thresholds. The speaker says some marketing of impact sensors was "unethical" (npgdKKdJSww [08:04]). Using GPS-unit collision output as a head-impact proxy is an inference this talk does not support.

**Example** — The speaker's own positional comparison: receivers under 400 impacts, linemen near or over 1,000 at about the same average force (npgdKKdJSww [18:51]). The caption at [18:51] ("th000") is garbled; the figure is as read.

=== framework--impact-alert-threshold-and-sideline-test-pairing.md
# Setting an impact-alert threshold: the S-curve and the sideline test it depends on

**What it is** — The speaker's way of reasoning about a helmet, headband or mouthpiece sensor with a red-light and green-light alert (npgdKKdJSww [08:04]). Risk of concussion against linear acceleration is an S-curve: the speaker knows of no concussion at 10 G, and concussion "everyone's going to get" at 300 G, with only a curve in between, so any alert line is arbitrary (npgdKKdJSww [08:04], [08:35]). The speaker walks the trade-off:
- Line at 50 G: the light "going off all the time", and every flagged athlete needs an evaluation.
- Line at 100 G: fewer alerts, but concussions at 60 or 70 G are missed.
- Line at 150 G: "once every few games", and "you're really not helping anybody" because most concussions happen at lower levels (npgdKKdJSww [08:35], [09:06]).

The alert is only usable if the follow-up test is fast. The speaker wants a sideline test under one minute so the line can be set low (the speaker mentions 80 or 100 G) without disrupting the game (npgdKKdJSww [09:06], [09:36]). The existing 20-minute evaluation (caption "SC stat too", likely SCAT2) "has never been validated" and its parts cannot decide return to play alone, and at a low yield (the speaker says "10%" actually concussed) "no one's going to use it" (npgdKKdJSww [09:36], [10:06]). The one fast test the speaker calls promising is King-Devick: two published papers (boxers, MMA fighters, college athletes at Penn) found concussions in under one minute by comparing to baseline (npgdKKdJSww [11:41]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives the logic of false alarms against misses but no data on any particular line. Inference: the threshold choice sets a false-alarm rate, and the false-alarm rate is only tolerable if the confirmation step is cheap, which makes the confirmation step the binding design constraint.

**When to apply** — Before anyone proposes alerts from impact sensors, GPS-unit collision counts or any single-number flag: state the line, the expected alerts per game, who evaluates each one, and how long that takes.

Eric's baseline: a measurement earns its place only if it answers a question someone has ("If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place," interview 2026-09-28, Q3, Explicit), and data collection is judged on cost against insight (Explicit, SportSmith 2026-02-19). Inference: an alert with no cheap follow-up fails both tests.

**When NOT to apply** — The speaker discloses a financial relationship with the owner of the King-Devick test (npgdKKdJSww [00:30]), and the "promising" claim rests on two papers the speaker does not name. The 10 G and 300 G anchors are stated without a source. The talk is from 2012 and the SCAT2 and King-Devick remarks may be out of date; check current guidelines. The caption "45C evaluation" at [11:41] to [12:12] is garbled. Return-to-play decisions belong to Athletic Medicine.

**Example** — The speaker's own: a line of 80 to 100 G with a one-minute baseline-comparison test, so that "you know immediately whether or not they can go back in" (npgdKKdJSww [09:36]). The speaker says this does not exist yet ("right now we don't have that").

**Related** — [[claim--diagnosed-concussion-rates-undercount-survey-and-observer-rates]]; [[framework--hit-count-as-exposure-budget-modeled-on-pitch-count]]; [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]] (Old Bull: what a sensor measures versus what is inferred from it).

# Diagnosed concussion rates sit far below what surveys and sideline observers find

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Chris nowinsky", who also gives his background as a former Harvard football player and pro wrestler, npgdKKdJSww [01:00]) says that programs with athletic trainers diagnose about 5% of athletes per year in contact and collision sports, "one out of 20", while anonymous end-of-season surveys that leave out the word "concussion" and ask about symptoms after blows give numbers "more like 50%" (npgdKKdJSww [06:04]). He cites three further results, all second-hand and with garbled study names:
- A study (caption "langbert") in which the average person suffered "three dings per season" (npgdKKdJSww [06:34]).
- A hockey study (caption "eckan") of 16 to 21 year olds in which a doctor placed in the stands liberally pulled players who looked off and tested them with the standard tools: the speaker reports the study author found 35% ("one-third were pulled out") versus 5% in the usual trainer-only group, "seven times as many" concussions (npgdKKdJSww [06:34], [07:04]).
- An observer study in which stand observers saw about half the symptoms players reported; the captions give 33 versus 54 for a women's sample, with the unit unstated, so the figures are unclear (npgdKKdJSww [07:04]).

From these he estimates "we are probably diagnosing between two and 10% of concussions" (npgdKKdJSww [07:34]). The estimate is the speaker's own, not a measured rate.

**Why it works** — The speaker's mechanism is that the injury cannot be seen: concussion does not show on standard CT or MRI and diagnosis rests on signs and symptoms, so sports "get by" without removing athletes the way they would for a visible injury (npgdKKdJSww [05:04], [07:34]). Inference: a diagnosis count measures reporting and detection effort as much as incidence, which is why putting a doctor in the stands moved the count sevenfold.

**When to apply** — When someone quotes a diagnosed-concussion rate as the incidence of the injury, or when judging whether an Athletic Medicine count captures most events. Inference: an anonymous symptom survey at season end, asked without the word "concussion", is the comparison the speaker's own data points to.

Eric's baseline: Applied Performance's part in return to play is testing and progression with shared loading decisions (Eric, interview 2026-09-28, Q4: "Testing and progression. I collaborate on loading and progression decisions when needed. It doesn't really end." Explicit), and no formal injury-risk model is in use (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). The baseline holds no concussion criteria, so this entry is a comparison point, not a method Eric uses.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not read 50% as the rate of medically diagnosable concussion; surveys count self-reported symptoms after blows. The hockey sample is 16 to 21 year olds, and the speaker gives no sample sizes for any of the three studies. The speaker discloses a consultant role and a financial tie to the owner of the King-Devick test (npgdKKdJSww [00:30]). The talk is from 2012, so detection practice and rules have changed since. Do not carry the rates to Baylor football without Athletic Medicine's own counts. Anything diagnostic belongs to Athletic Medicine; Applied Performance does not set concussion criteria.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the hockey study, where adding one observer with pull-out authority took the identified share from 5% to 35% (npgdKKdJSww [06:34], [07:04]).

**Related** — [[framework--impact-alert-threshold-and-sideline-test-pairing]]; [[claim--perfect-concussion-detection-would-sideline-one-fifth-of-players]] (the speaker's own consequence of closing this gap); [[claim--concussion-vulnerability-window-longer-than-return-rules-assumed]]; [[funk-2025-an-analysis-of-guardian-cap-use-and-changes-in-the-concussion-rate-in-national-football-le]] (NFL preseason practice concussion rates, an exposure-based cohort).

# If every concussion were caught and managed strictly, about one in five players would be out at any time

**What it is** — A back-of-envelope availability model. The speaker, using the survey figure that about half of athletes have a concussion each year, takes a 50-person football team with half concussed (25 players) and 10 days out each: 250 days, "about 4% of playing days", "not completely disruptive" (npgdKKdJSww [12:12]). The speaker then argues recovery is longer than 10 days (see the vulnerability-window entry) and reruns it at 60 days out: "21% of playing days", "one out of five athletes out at all times", about four of a football team's starters and one hockey starter at any moment, not counting repeat concussions (npgdKKdJSww [13:43], [14:14]). The speaker's conclusion is that either medical guidelines get much looser ("which won't happen") or the games change, starting with how much contact they contain (npgdKKdJSww [14:45], [22:58]).

The speaker says the math was done "on the plane" and that "the science is iffy" on the 10-day figure (npgdKKdJSww [12:12]).

**Why it works** — It is arithmetic on three assumed inputs: incidence, days out, and playing days in a season. The speaker gives the first two and not the third. Inference: 250 days equal 4% only if the team has about 6,250 player-days (50 players over about 125 days), and the 60-day case then gives 1,500 days over 6,250, or 24%, not the 21% the speaker states; the two figures are not exactly proportional and the denominator is not shown. Treat both as rough.

**When to apply** — As a reminder to test a proposed detection or return-to-play standard against roster availability before adopting it: ask what the standard would cost in player-days if applied to every case.

Eric's baseline: Applied Performance's role in return to performance is to supply information that supports Athletic Medicine and Athletic Performance decisions (Explicit, Playbook p.6), and Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q22): "We don't assess readiness. The template answers that." (Explicit). Inference: an availability estimate like this one is the kind of information Applied Performance could supply; the clearance standard itself stays with Athletic Medicine.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use the 4% or 21% figures as estimates for Baylor or for any real team. The 50% incidence is a survey figure from the speaker's other studies; the 10-day and 60-day recoveries are assumptions, and the 60-day case is the speaker's hypothetical of what very sensitive tests might demand, not a clinical standard. The model ignores repeat concussions, position differences and substitutions. It is a 2012 talk, and the speaker discloses a consultant role and a test-owner tie (npgdKKdJSww [00:30]).

**Example** — The speaker's own: a 50-person football team, 25 concussed, 60 days out each, "four guys out on your football team every week out of your starting group" (npgdKKdJSww [14:14]).

**Related** — [[claim--diagnosed-concussion-rates-undercount-survey-and-observer-rates]] (source of the 50% input); [[claim--concussion-vulnerability-window-longer-than-return-rules-assumed]] (source of the 30 to 60 day input); [[claim--practice-contact-is-the-largest-exposure-lever-in-football]] (the lever the speaker proposes in response).

# Cutting contact in practice is the main lever on head-impact exposure

**What it is** — The speaker's stated focus is "reducing hitting in practice", the "number one way" to restrict total counts, because in football "up to 75%" of brain trauma exposure happens in practice (npgdKKdJSww [19:23]). The speaker gives three policy moves as evidence that people are "buying in":
- In the NFL collective bargaining talks the players' union pushed for 14 practice days with contact in 18 weeks (npgdKKdJSww [19:23]).
- The Ivy League followed: NCAA rules allow five days of hitting a week and the Ivy League chose two, with an intent to push lower (npgdKKdJSww [19:54]).
- Pop Warner's executive director announced a plan to cut hitting from six hours a week to two by the next season (npgdKKdJSww [19:54]).

The speaker says "I was on both committees" (the captions do not name which) and "pushed these like crazy" (npgdKKdJSww [19:54]), and that some limit on how many contact sports a child plays in a year is likely to follow (npgdKKdJSww [20:24]).

**Why it works** — The speaker states that most of the exposure comes in practice (npgdKKdJSww [19:23]) and gives no further reasoning. Inference: practices outnumber games, so most hits occur there. The 75% figure comes with no source or method in the talk. Inference: contact in practice is also the exposure a program controls directly, which is why it is a lever where game contact is not.

**When to apply** — When a contact-practice schedule is being set or reviewed and the discussion is about how many contact periods, not about equipment. Inference: Applied Performance could log contact periods per practice by position group (practice minutes with contact, not impacts) and report them weekly to Athletic Medicine and coaches, as a record, not a cap.

Eric's baseline: "Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver" (Inferred (transcript)). In the in-season game week, lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q15). The baseline holds no contact-practice rule and no concussion criteria.

**When NOT to apply** — The 75% is an assertion, and it is "up to" for football only (npgdKKdJSww [19:23]). The three policy examples are the speaker's account of NFL, Ivy League and youth practice, with the speaker involved in two of them; none reports an outcome. College or Baylor practice schedules are not described, and contact definitions would have to be agreed with coaches. The talk gives no evidence that limiting contact reduces concussions; it gives the exposure logic and the policy trend. A contact-practice decision is the coaching staff's with Athletic Medicine; Applied Performance supplies the count.

**Example** — The speaker's own: Pop Warner moving from six hours of weekly contact to two (npgdKKdJSww [19:54]).

**Related** — [[framework--hit-count-as-exposure-budget-modeled-on-pitch-count]]; [[claim--perfect-concussion-detection-would-sideline-one-fifth-of-players]]; [[funk-2025-an-analysis-of-guardian-cap-use-and-changes-in-the-concussion-rate-in-national-football-le]] (NFL preseason practice concussion rates).
