=== case-study--spring-training-field-lab-post-surgery-vs-never-injured.md
confidence: supported

# Spring training field lab: pitchers back from UCL surgery looked mechanically like never-injured pitchers

**What it is** — Glenn Fleisig describes a study done with Major League Baseball in the 2014 spring training in Arizona and Florida, where the speaker's group brought the motion-capture lab (in a tent or outdoors) to the teams instead of bringing pitchers to Birmingham (AgouMNTeyo4 [25:16], [26:17]). Design: 40 pitchers who had had the surgery a couple of years earlier and had made it back to spring training, against 40 never-injured pitchers; each filled out a form, had range of motion measured lying on a table, then had a full kinematics and kinetics test (AgouMNTeyo4 [25:47], [26:17], [26:47]).

The speaker named four hypotheses before looking (AgouMNTeyo4 [26:47], [27:18], [27:49], [28:21]):
- The returners show compensation, "messed up" elbow and shoulder mechanics.
- They hold back: stand more upright and push their elbow.
- The "inverted W": the arm is late and still down at foot contact, measured as arm external rotation at foot contact.
- A low elbow that is then raised, a stressful pattern.

Result: both groups threw about 85 mph in spring training and matched on height and weight; the speaker found no difference in flexibility and no difference in mechanics (AgouMNTeyo4 [28:21], [28:52]). The speaker's reading: minor leaguers who make it back have typical flexibility and mechanics, "when it works it works" (AgouMNTeyo4 [28:52], [29:22]).

**Why it works** — The design works because it names each hypothesis as a measurable pattern before testing; the speaker gives no mechanism for the null result. Inference: if returners were compensating, the group means would differ on the four named patterns, and they did not.

**When to apply** — As a template for a field comparison of a return group against matched controls: define the comparison group, name hypotheses as measurable patterns in advance, and take the lab to the athletes when the athletes cannot come to the lab.

Eric's baseline: Applied Performance's contribution to return to performance is "Testing and progression" with shared loading decisions (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q4); testing must be repeatable ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April," Inferred (transcript)). The baseline does not document a return-group comparison at Baylor.

**When NOT to apply** — Fleisig lists the limits: only minor leaguers were studied, only after they made it back (no pre-injury mechanics), and only success stories, not the "10 or 20%" who did not return (AgouMNTeyo4 [28:52], [29:22], [29:53]). A null result in 40 against 40 does not exclude small differences, and the talk gives no effect sizes. At the time of the talk the study had "just got published". Baseball pitchers only; do not infer a football return standard. The group is selected on having come back healthy.

**Example** — The speaker's own: a never-injured pitcher and a returner both at about 85 mph, indistinguishable on the four patterns (AgouMNTeyo4 [28:21]).

**Related** — [[claim--post-ucl-surgery-return-rate-and-performance-studies-disagree]]; [[framework--proper-mechanics-as-reference-range-of-healthy-fast-pitchers]]; [[framework--prospective-baseline-then-follow-cohort-from-the-draft]] (a design that would capture the pre-injury data this study lacked; Inference).
=== claim--curveballs-not-shown-more-stressful-than-fastballs.md
confidence: supported

# A failed attempt to prove that curveballs are more dangerous than fastballs

**What it is** — Glenn Fleisig says ASMI had advised for years not to throw curveballs until the growth plates close ("don't throw curve balls until you're old enough to shave") and ran studies to prove it (AgouMNTeyo4 [38:40], [39:11]). The result went the other way:
- Lab: in three biomechanics studies (two in Birmingham, one in Connecticut, some by other groups), elbow torque in a curveball was the same as or a little less than in a fastball (AgouMNTeyo4 [39:11], [39:41]).
- Field: in the 10-year cohort of about 500 youth pitchers, those who started throwing curveballs younger were not the ones who got hurt (AgouMNTeyo4 [40:12]).
- Conclusion: "we have not proven that the curve ball is dangerous. We have proven pitching too much is dangerous" (AgouMNTeyo4 [40:12], [40:42]).

In Q&A the speaker is careful: failing to prove danger is not proving safety, so young pitchers should still learn a fastball and a changeup first and add a curveball "when you're ready", because the purpose of off-speed pitches is to disturb the batter's timing (AgouMNTeyo4 [52:31], [53:02]). On pitch type, the speaker's group has studied fastballs, curveballs, changeups and sliders: fastballs, curveballs and sliders are stressful, changeups less so; split-fingered fastballs were not studied (AgouMNTeyo4 [53:02]).

**Why it works** — Fleisig's measure of stress is elbow torque calculated from motion capture: kinematics (positions and angles) from cameras and kinetics (forces) calculated by equation, torque of about 100 N·m at one arm position shown on screen ("when the arm gets in this position"; the captions do not name the position or the pitch type) (AgouMNTeyo4 [11:46], [12:17], [15:27]). Inference: if torque is the right proxy for ligament load, a pitch with equal torque should carry equal ligament risk; the speaker does not test that proxy in this talk (the speaker says the link from arm stress to injury is unproven, AgouMNTeyo4 [58:38]).

**When to apply** — As a worked example of a prior belief tested by two designs (lab mechanics and field cohort) and reported when it failed. Also when a coaching rule rests on tradition: ask what the stress measure and the field outcome actually show.

Eric's baseline: Applied Performance's mission is to help the team "answer questions, ask better questions, and discover new ones" rather than hand down answers unilaterally (Explicit, Playbook p.6). Inference: Fleisig reversing a position the speaker's own center had held is the posture that mission describes.
**When NOT to apply** — Baseball pitching in youth to professional levels; the torque comparison does not transfer to any football skill. The speaker does not show the torque numbers for the three curveball studies or the cohort statistics, so the "same or less" result is as stated. "Not proven dangerous" is not "safe", as the speaker says (AgouMNTeyo4 [52:31]). The cohort is the same one that shows the 100-innings result, and the tested pitches did not include the split-finger. A rule about when to introduce a pitch is a coaching and medical decision; do not remove an age guideline on this result alone.

**Example** — The speaker's own contrast: ASMI's advice before the studies against its results (AgouMNTeyo4 [39:11], [40:42]).

**Related** — [[claim--youth-pitching-over-100-innings-triples-serious-injury-risk]] (same cohort); [[principle--throwing-harder-raises-risk-and-performance]] (the 2017 speaker on fastball usage and velocity as risk factors); [[framework--proper-mechanics-as-reference-range-of-healthy-fast-pitchers]].
=== claim--pitching-while-fatigued-is-the-largest-retrospective-odds.md
confidence: supported

# Pitchers who often pitch while fatigued carry the largest odds of having had elbow surgery

**What it is** — Glenn Fleisig compares pitchers who came in for surgery with pitchers who never had surgery, asking about their backgrounds (AgouMNTeyo4 [31:58], [32:30]). He frames the answers as bets: someone who often threw more than 80 pitches in a game: "4 to 1" that the person has the scar; someone who pitched more than 8 months a year: "5 to 1" (the "8 months" is caption-dependent); someone who often pitched when fatigued: "36 to 1" (the caption reads "$36 to $1" and "3600%") (AgouMNTeyo4 [32:30], [33:00], [33:31]). The speaker calls the fatigue result "the biggest result I found" in all of the speaker's studies and says "you could throw everything else away" and keep it: pitchers who keep pitching after they are fatigued end up with serious injury (AgouMNTeyo4 [33:31]).

**Why it works** — Fleisig gives no mechanism. Inference: fatigue is a state in which each additional pitch is thrown with less control, which would plausibly add stress; the speaker does not say this, and this comparison used history, not mechanics.

**When to apply** — When the question is which exposure is the most modifiable for a throwing athlete's history: fatigue behavior (continuing when tired) and volume (pitches per game, months per year). Pair with the prospective 100-innings result rather than using the odds alone.

Eric's baseline: a trained coach's eye is treated as at least as important as technology for daily assessment (Inferred, transcript, speaker unconfirmed); the eye flags where to look and data then investigates ("There is a place for the coach's eye: when something looks off, it can direct you where to look and gather data to investigate further," interview 2026-09-28, Q6, Explicit). Daily subjective wellness surveys were dropped for general roster use because athletes gamed them, and are kept for return to play and chronic conditions (Explicit, SportSmith 2026-02-19). Inference: the speaker's "fatigued" is a history item the athlete reports; Eric's survey experience is a reason to doubt a self-reported fatigue score used daily.

**When NOT to apply** — These are retrospective odds from recalled history, not a prospective rate: there is no control for who tells the story, for when pitchers were asked, or for who came in for surgery in the first place. The speaker states the odds as spoken wagers and gives no sample size for this retrospective comparison (the 500 kids belong to the separate 10-year prospective study), no confidence interval and no definition of "often" or "fatigued". In the Q&A the speaker says scientific measurement of fatigue (muscle activity) does not work and that it cannot be figured out at the moment of the game (AgouMNTeyo4 [49:59], [50:29]). The caption wording of the three odds ("8 months", "$36 to $1") is uncertain. Do not treat 36 to 1 as an individual risk score or transfer it to football. The speaker says the speaker is an adviser for Little League, Major League Baseball, many teams, USA Baseball and a company (AgouMNTeyo4 [06:08]).

**Example** — The speaker's own device: the speaker imagines half a room with elbow scars and half without, asks each person whether they often pitched when fatigued, and says a "yes" is a 36 to 1 bet that the person is in the scar group (paraphrase of AgouMNTeyo4 [32:30] to [33:31]; the caption is garbled).

**Related** — [[claim--youth-pitching-over-100-innings-triples-serious-injury-risk]]; [[heuristic--fatigue-is-individual-read-it-next-day-with-trainer-knowledge]] (the speaker's Q&A answer on how to see fatigue); [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]] (Old Bull).
=== claim--post-ucl-surgery-return-rate-and-performance-studies-disagree.md
confidence: contested

# After UCL ("Tommy John") surgery, about 80% return, but whether performance rises is disputed

**What it is** — Glenn Fleisig (title spelling; caption "fleig") of the American Sports Medicine Institute (ASMI) reviews what happens to pitchers after ulnar collateral ligament reconstruction (AgouMNTeyo4 [06:08]).

Return and time:
- Three studies in the same journal, on largely the same pitchers, tracked how pitchers did afterward: one covering 1974 to 2012, one of 147 pitchers since 1999, one of the 38 most recent pitchers with PitchFX data since 2008 (caption names "Ericson", "mcne", "Jang"; spellings unverified) (AgouMNTeyo4 [20:04], [20:35], [21:05]).
- About 80% of major leaguers return, 20% do not; in the middle study 80% made it back for at least one game but only about 67% "made it back and stayed there" (AgouMNTeyo4 [22:10], [22:40]).
- Published studies put the return to the majors at about a year and a half; ASMI's own data (Dr Andrews' patients, major league, minor league or amateur) show about 80% return in about 12 months, and he explains the gap as waiting for the next season (AgouMNTeyo4 [22:40], [24:15]).
- Age at surgery does not change the roughly 80% chance of returning to the same level or higher (high school, college, pro), but for a 16 year old "we don't have enough long-term data" and he calls it "a worrisome road" (AgouMNTeyo4 [56:34], [57:05]).

Performance: the first study said pitchers got better after surgery; the other two did not, finding performance "down like controls", that is, as an age-matched decline would predict. Fleisig says "I kind of believe" the second and third (AgouMNTeyo4 [21:05], [21:39], [22:10]). Returning to a slide he says he did not show earlier, he says "their stats went down like the controls" (referent unclear in the captions: it may be the ASMI subgroup or the cited studies) (AgouMNTeyo4 [23:11], [23:43]).

Definitions of success: the cited studies used at least 10 major league games; Fleisig says he would define success as staying healthy (off the disabled list, no repeat surgery) and statistics that match the age group (AgouMNTeyo4 [53:32], [54:02], [54:32]).

**Why it works** — Fleisig's explanation for the performance disagreement is age: pitchers having surgery at 30 or 33 would naturally decline, so comparing to the pre-surgery self overstates the change (AgouMNTeyo4 [21:39]). Inference: the three studies differ in who is counted and in what the comparator is, which is why a trajectory matched to age or role is the better yardstick.

**When to apply** — When defining what "back" means for an athlete returning from a major surgery: define it by several criteria, set the comparison to an age- and role-expected path, and state the time window before anyone judges the return.

Eric's baseline: Applied Performance supports return-to-performance decisions with information (Explicit, Playbook p.6), contributes "Testing and progression" with shared loading decisions, and the involvement "doesn't really end" (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q4, Q4a). A written protocol exists in the UE and LE rehab templates, but Flint has not read them. Inference: Fleisig's multi-part success definition could be set against those templates once staged; the baseline does not hold return criteria.

**When NOT to apply** — Elbow reconstruction in baseball pitchers only; do not transfer the 80%, 67% or 12 to 18 month figures to football or to other injuries. The 16% prevalence and 25% major league figures and the ASMI return data come from a study he says is unpublished or from his own center (AgouMNTeyo4 [08:13], [23:11]). The three-study summary has garbled author names, and the speaker says he is not a medical doctor (AgouMNTeyo4 [19:33]). The first study disagrees with the other two on performance; the 2017 speaker says the medical research shows no performance gain, which sides with the latter two (sHXuxj3-rbQ [06:17]), and reports that, preliminarily, players with a second surgery came back less strongly (sHXuxj3-rbQ [04:12]). The 10-game bar may be low for a star pitcher.

**Example** — The speaker's own, from the Q&A: asked how to define success for two high-profile returning pitchers, he said the studies' bar was at least 10 major league games, that some injured pitchers were marginal major leaguers to begin with, which makes that a reasonable criterion for them, and that he would define success as staying healthy and statistics matching the age group (AgouMNTeyo4 [53:32], [54:02], [54:32]).

**Related** — [[claim--surgery-misperceptions-among-youth-players-and-parents]] (what players expect the surgery to do, from a 2017 talk that cites a survey also shown here at [18:30]); [[framework--prospective-baseline-then-follow-cohort-from-the-draft]]; [[principle--competitive-exposure-required-before-return-to-play]] (Harries); [[claim--ucl-reconstruction-return-outcomes-mlb-pitchers]] (closest related entry, a 2019 talk on return outcomes in MLB pitchers).
=== claim--youth-pitching-over-100-innings-triples-serious-injury-risk.md
confidence: supported

# Youth pitchers with over 100 competitive innings in a year had more than three times the serious-injury risk

**What it is** — Glenn Fleisig reports a prospective cohort from his center (ASMI): about 500 youth pitchers were called every week during a season (the caption says "spring training season") to ask how much they pitched and whether the elbow or shoulder hurt, then called once a year for 10 years, "started out as little kids" and ended as about 22 year olds or out of the game (AgouMNTeyo4 [31:28]). Result: pitchers who pitched more than 100 innings in competition in any year of the study were "more than three times" as likely to have a serious elbow or shoulder injury needing surgery or making them quit baseball (AgouMNTeyo4 [31:58]). His one-line takeaway from all his data: "too much pitching leads to injury" (AgouMNTeyo4 [34:02]). Throwing is natural, but "excessive pitching is not natural": 100 full-effort pitches every fifth day is not (AgouMNTeyo4 [34:32]).

The 2017 league-office speaker cites a ten-year youth study with the same finding, 100 or more innings in a year, and does not name it (sHXuxj3-rbQ [07:54]); the two talks probably refer to the same work, which neither confirms.

**Why it works** — Fleisig gives no mechanism for the innings threshold. Inference: it is a volume exposure that the study measured weekly, which is what makes it more than a recall finding.

**When to apply** — As the evidence base for any exposure cap on overhead throwing in youth baseball, and as the model for how to get exposure evidence: a defined cohort, short-interval exposure logging, long follow-up.

Eric's baseline: "Injury risk can be reduced, not eliminated, through sound programming, progression, and collaboration with Athletic Medicine" (Inferred (transcript); course team position, individual speaker unconfirmed). Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q12): "We don't have any formal risk model that we follow." (Explicit, interview-confirmed). Inference: this is cohort evidence for a dose, which is a different thing from an ACWR model Eric does not trust.

**When NOT to apply** — Youth baseball pitchers only; the speaker is explicit that these are kids who "started out as little kids". Do not set a college or professional innings limit from 100. The talk gives no confidence interval, adjustment for confounders or counts of injuries, so the "more than three times" is as stated, not a fitted estimate. Fleisig reports his own center's study and says he advises Little League, many MLB teams, USA Baseball and a company captioned "modus," whose gadgets he is helping develop (AgouMNTeyo4 [06:08], [41:13]). # Fatigue is individual: read it with people who know the athlete, and read it the next day

**What it is** — Asked how coaches and parents know when a pitcher has reached the fatigue level, the speaker answers in Q&A (the talk is titled with Glenn Fleisig; the captions carry no speaker labels) (AgouMNTeyo4 [49:59], [50:29]):

- What is decided is not at game time but afterward: in the training room the trainers are "a key for reading when a guy is better, when it is normal and when it's not normal". A pitcher who used to need two days of recovery and now needs three is a signal; the speaker says pro teams will skip or bump a start on trainer feedback (AgouMNTeyo4 [51:00], [51:30]).
- The athlete's education is for the next day: pain in the elbow or shoulder is not normal; full-body fatigue is normal; feeling full-body fatigue in the game "is your body saying let's call it a day" (AgouMNTeyo4 [51:30], [52:01]).
- Summary line: "fatigue is individual" (AgouMNTeyo4 [51:30]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism and no data for this answer; it is the speaker's stated practice among the pro teams and trainers the speaker talks to. Inference: it uses the one signal the speaker points to, a person who sees the athlete every day and compares to that athlete's own normal, which fits a result that fatigue behavior was the largest risk marker while no instrument measured it.

**When to apply** — When a monitoring system needs an escalation path: define who reads the athlete the next day, what counts as a change from his own normal (recovery taking longer, pain versus tiredness), and what action follows a flag.

Eric's baseline: the coach's eye flags where to look and data then investigates (interview 2026-09-28, Q6, Explicit); a trained eye is treated as at least as important as technology for daily assessment (Inferred (transcript)). Daily subjective wellness surveys were dropped for general roster use because athletes gamed them, kept for return to play and chronic conditions (Explicit, SportSmith 2026-02-19), and mRSI from daily CMJ testing replaced them as the readiness marker (Explicit, same source). Inference: the answer partly conflicts with the mRSI choice, since it relies on trainer and athlete report; Eric's practice keeps subjective input only where context is needed, such as return to play. Recovery is managed through load design, with nothing objective tracked (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q23).

It presumes trainers or coaches who see the athlete daily and a written trigger for what happens after a flag. Pitching context: one start every fifth day, with a next-day check; do not copy the "next day" timing to football's weekly cycle without Baylor's own staff routine. Self-report can be gamed (Eric's survey experience above). Fatigue and pain are not distinguished by any test in the talk.

# Spring training field lab: pitchers back from UCL surgery looked mechanically like never-injured pitchers

**What it is** — Glenn Fleisig describes a study done with Major League Baseball in the 2014 spring training in Arizona and Florida, where the speaker's group brought the motion-capture lab (in a tent or outdoors) to the teams instead of bringing pitchers to Birmingham (AgouMNTeyo4 [25:16], [26:17]). Design: 40 pitchers who had had the surgery a couple of years earlier and had made it back to spring training, against 40 never-injured pitchers; each filled out a form, had range of motion measured lying on a table, then had a full kinematics and kinetics test (AgouMNTeyo4 [25:47], [26:17], [26:47]).

The speaker named four hypotheses before looking (AgouMNTeyo4 [26:47], [27:18], [27:49], [28:21]):
- The returners show compensation, "messed up" elbow and shoulder mechanics.
- They hold back: stand more upright and push their elbow.
- The "inverted W": the arm is late and still down at foot contact, measured as arm external rotation at foot contact.
- A low elbow that is then raised, a stressful pattern.

Result: both groups threw about 85 mph in spring training and matched on height and weight; the speaker found no difference in flexibility and no difference in mechanics (AgouMNTeyo4 [28:21], [28:52]). The speaker's reading: minor leaguers who make it back have typical flexibility and mechanics, "when it works it works" (AgouMNTeyo4 [28:52], [29:22]).

**Why it works** — The design works because it names each hypothesis as a measurable pattern before testing; the speaker gives no mechanism for the null result. Inference: if returners were compensating, the group means would differ on the four named patterns, and they did not.

**When to apply** — As a template for a field comparison of a return group against matched controls: define the comparison group, name hypotheses as measurable patterns in advance, and take the lab to the athletes when the athletes cannot come to the lab.

Eric's baseline: Applied Performance's contribution to return to performance is "Testing and progression" with shared loading decisions (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q4); testing must be repeatable ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April," Inferred (transcript)). The baseline does not document a return-group comparison at Baylor.

**When NOT to apply** — Fleisig lists the limits: only minor leaguers were studied, only after they made it back (no pre-injury mechanics), and only success stories, not the "10 or 20%" who did not return (AgouMNTeyo4 [28:52], [29:22], [29:53]). A null result in 40 against 40 does not exclude small differences, and the talk gives no effect sizes. At the time of the talk the study had "just got published". Baseball pitchers only; do not infer a football return standard. The group is selected on having come back healthy.

**Example** — The speaker's own: a never-injured pitcher and a returner both at about 85 mph, indistinguishable on the four patterns (AgouMNTeyo4 [28:21]).

**Related** — [[claim--post-ucl-surgery-return-rate-and-performance-studies-disagree]]; [[framework--proper-mechanics-as-reference-range-of-healthy-fast-pitchers]]; [[framework--prospective-baseline-then-follow-cohort-from-the-draft]] (a design that would capture the pre-injury data this study lacked; Inference).

# Fatigue is individual: read it with people who know the athlete, and read it the next day

**What it is** — Asked how coaches and parents know when a pitcher has reached the fatigue level, the speaker answers in Q&A (the talk is titled with Glenn Fleisig; the captions carry no speaker labels) (AgouMNTeyo4 [49:59], [50:29]):
- The answer says they tried to measure fatigue scientifically from muscle activity, "it doesn't work".
- Pitcher and coach cannot figure it out at the moment of the game; they need to know each other beforehand (a tough guy, recent problems, how he walks after getting hurt), and no one wants a player pitching while thinking "I think it hurts a little" (AgouMNTeyo4 [50:29]).
- What is decided is not at game time but afterward: in the training room the trainers are "a key for reading when a guy is better, when it is normal and when it's not normal". A pitcher who used to need two days of recovery and now needs three is a signal; the speaker says pro teams will skip or bump a start on trainer feedback (AgouMNTeyo4 [51:00], [51:30]).
- The athlete's education is for the next day: pain in the elbow or shoulder is not normal; full-body fatigue is normal; feeling full-body fatigue in the game "is your body saying let's call it a day" (AgouMNTeyo4 [51:30], [52:01]).
- Summary line: "fatigue is individual" (AgouMNTeyo4 [51:30]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism and no data for this answer; it is the speaker's stated practice among the pro teams and trainers the speaker talks to. Inference: it uses the one signal the speaker points to, a person who sees the athlete every day and compares to that athlete's own normal, which fits a result that fatigue behavior was the largest risk marker while no instrument measured it.

**When to apply** — When a monitoring system needs an escalation path: define who reads the athlete the next day, what counts as a change from his own normal (recovery taking longer, pain versus tiredness), and what action follows a flag.

Eric's baseline: the coach's eye flags where to look and data then investigates (interview 2026-09-28, Q6, Explicit); a trained eye is treated as at least as important as technology for daily assessment (Inferred (transcript)). Daily subjective wellness surveys were dropped for general roster use because athletes gamed them, kept for return to play and chronic conditions (Explicit, SportSmith 2026-02-19), and mRSI from daily CMJ testing replaced them as the readiness marker (Explicit, same source). Inference: the answer partly conflicts with the mRSI choice, since it relies on trainer and athlete report; Eric's practice keeps subjective input only where context is needed, such as return to play. Recovery is managed through load design, with nothing objective tracked (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q23).

**When NOT to apply** — Assertion from one expert answer, not tested; the speaker says that measurement attempts failed. It presumes trainers or coaches who see the athlete daily and a written trigger for what happens after a flag. Pitching context: one start every fifth day, with a next-day check; do not copy the "next day" timing to football's weekly cycle without Baylor's own staff routine. Self-report can be gamed (Eric's survey experience above). Fatigue and pain are not distinguished by any test in the talk.

**Example** — The speaker's own: a pitcher whose recovery moved from two days to three, which the trainer notices and which can lead the team to skip a start (AgouMNTeyo4 [51:00], [51:30]).

**Related** — [[claim--pitching-while-fatigued-is-the-largest-retrospective-odds]]; [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] (Old Bull).

# Defining "proper mechanics" as the mean and spread of healthy, high-velocity pitchers

**What it is** — Asked how he knows what proper mechanics are, Glenn Fleisig describes his criteria: the pitcher came to his lab, had not been injured for at least a year, and had a high fastball velocity during the test (AgouMNTeyo4 [54:32], [55:03]). He took about 150 such pitchers (by his account including Roger Clemens, and "some college guy you never heard of"), computed the mean and standard deviation of each measurement (stride length is his example), and calls that range proper mechanics: in effect the 150 best pitchers he has tested by ball velocity (AgouMNTeyo4 [55:03], [55:33]; the caption says "pictures", read here as pitchers). Studies then showed pitchers outside those ranges, as a group, had lower ball velocity and higher stress on the arm (AgouMNTeyo4 [55:33], [56:03]). He has also tested over 2,000 pitchers in the lab, including eight who went on to win Cy Young awards (caption "sa young", "15 sa young Awards"), with 12 cameras and about 40 markers (AgouMNTeyo4 [13:20], [13:51], [43:13]).

His own account of the limits: when asked whether pitchers measured with poor mechanics later got hurt, "it was a mixed bag", about half did and half did not. He says mechanics is only one factor, that his lab intervenes by telling pitchers what they do wrong (so some may fix it), and that the step from higher arm stress to more injury is "a leap of faith" that he has not proven (AgouMNTeyo4 [58:06], [58:38]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's logic is that good mechanics give more velocity and less arm stress, and bad mechanics more stress (AgouMNTeyo4 [24:45]). Inference: the benchmark is built from a selected, healthy, fast group, so a measure outside the range is a flag for a closer look, not a finding of risk.

**When to apply** — Inference: building a reference range for any lab or field metric: define the reference group by outcome criteria (healthy for a stated time, high performance on a stated test), report the mean and standard deviation of each variable, and test whether being outside the range predicts the thing you care about.

Eric's baseline: force plate and monitoring thresholds are individualized, not fixed positional cut-offs: "Wednesdays, the thresholds should be individualized," against percent change from baseline or a rolling average, with standard deviations and the smallest worthwhile change used "to diagnose signal versus noise" (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q2, Q2a). Metrics are chosen by the output, driver, strategy and optional symmetry framework from Hawkin Dynamics (adopted practice, framework not Eric's own). Inference: Fleisig's group reference range is a between-athlete benchmark, where Eric's thresholds compare an athlete to his own baseline, so the two answer different questions. No sport- or position-specific thresholds exist formally at Baylor (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q7).

**When NOT to apply** — The benchmark is partly circular: "proper" is defined by high velocity and health, then the finding that people outside the range throw slower is close to built in. The follow-up on injury was mixed and unproven by his own account. The lab is baseball pitching. Do not use an out-of-range value to restrict an athlete by itself. The group's size (about 150) is stated, the criteria for "high velocity" are not, and results for the unpublished spring-training work are separate. Fleisig says of a company the caption spells "modus", "I am personally helping them develop some uh some gadgets to measure things" (AgouMNTeyo4 [41:13]); the devices in the talk were not validated in it.

**Example** — The speaker's own: stride length, where one pitcher's value is one number and another's another, and the group mean and standard deviation define the proper range (AgouMNTeyo4 [55:33]).

**Related** — [[claim--curveballs-not-shown-more-stressful-than-fastballs]]; [[case-study--spring-training-field-lab-post-surgery-vs-never-injured]] (field use of the same lab); [[principle--throwing-harder-raises-risk-and-performance]].

# A failed attempt to prove that curveballs are more dangerous than fastballs

**What it is** — Glenn Fleisig says ASMI had advised for years not to throw curveballs until the growth plates close ("don't throw curve balls until you're old enough to shave") and ran studies to prove it (AgouMNTeyo4 [38:40], [39:11]). The result went the other way:
- Lab: in three biomechanics studies (two in Birmingham, one in Connecticut, some by other groups), elbow torque in a curveball was the same as or a little less than in a fastball (AgouMNTeyo4 [39:11], [39:41]).
- Field: in the 10-year cohort of about 500 youth pitchers, those who started throwing curveballs younger were not the ones who got hurt (AgouMNTeyo4 [40:12]).
- Conclusion: "we have not proven that the curve ball is dangerous. We have proven pitching too much is dangerous" (AgouMNTeyo4 [40:12], [40:42]).

In Q&A the speaker is careful: failing to prove danger is not proving safety, so young pitchers should still learn a fastball and a changeup first and add a curveball "when you're ready", because the purpose of off-speed pitches is to disturb the batter's timing (AgouMNTeyo4 [52:31], [53:02]). On pitch type, the speaker's group has studied fastballs, curveballs, changeups and sliders: fastballs, curveballs and sliders are stressful, changeups less so; split-fingered fastballs were not studied (AgouMNTeyo4 [53:02]).

**Why it works** — Fleisig's measure of stress is elbow torque calculated from motion capture: kinematics (positions and angles) from cameras and kinetics (forces) calculated by equation, torque of about 100 N·m at one arm position shown on screen ("when the arm gets in this position"; the captions do not name the position or the pitch type) (AgouMNTeyo4 [11:46], [12:17], [15:27]). Inference: if torque is the right proxy for ligament load, a pitch with equal torque should carry equal ligament risk; the speaker does not test that proxy in this talk (the speaker says the link from arm stress to injury is unproven, AgouMNTeyo4 [58:38]).

**When to apply** — As a worked example of a prior belief tested by two designs (lab mechanics and field cohort) and reported when it failed. Also when a coaching rule rests on tradition: ask what the stress measure and the field outcome actually show.

Eric's baseline: Applied Performance's mission is to help the team "answer questions, ask better questions, and discover new ones" rather than hand down answers unilaterally (Explicit, Playbook p.6). Inference: Fleisig reversing a position the speaker's own center had held is the posture that mission describes.
**When NOT to apply** — Baseball pitching in youth to professional levels; the torque comparison does not transfer to any football skill. The speaker does not show the torque numbers for the three curveball studies or the cohort statistics, so the "same or less" result is as stated. "Not proven dangerous" is not "safe", as the speaker says (AgouMNTeyo4 [52:31]). The cohort is the same one that shows the 100-innings result, and the tested pitches did not include the split-finger. A rule about when to introduce a pitch is a coaching and medical decision; do not remove an age guideline on this result alone.

**Example** — The speaker's own contrast: ASMI's advice before the studies against its results (AgouMNTeyo4 [39:11], [40:42]).

**Related** — [[claim--youth-pitching-over-100-innings-triples-serious-injury-risk]] (same cohort); [[principle--throwing-harder-raises-risk-and-performance]] (the 2017 speaker on fastball usage and velocity as risk factors); [[framework--proper-mechanics-as-reference-range-of-healthy-fast-pitchers]].
